---
title: "Lecture 8: Bonds with Embedded Options"
subtitle: "Callable valuation, option-adjusted spread, and effective risk"
author: "BUS 411"
---

## Embedded options make cash flows state dependent

For an option-free bond, promised cash flows are fixed. For a callable bond, falling rates can cause the issuer to redeem early.

Valuation must model both **future rates** and the **exercise rule**.

## Traditional yield spread mixes several effects

$$\text{Yield spread}=YTM_{bond}-YTM_{benchmark}$$

Drawbacks:

- one YTM discounts many dates,
- benchmark cash flows differ,
- the spread includes option cost,
- expected cash flows change with rates.

## Static spread improves cash-flow timing

The static spread $s$ solves:

$$P=\sum_t\frac{CF_t}{(1+z_t+s)^t}$$

Each cash flow uses its spot rate plus one constant spread. This works when cash flows are known—but callable cash flows are not.

## Callability transfers value to the issuer

When rates fall, the issuer can refinance at a lower cost. The investor receives the call price and loses the valuable above-market coupon stream.

Therefore a callable bond is worth less than an otherwise identical option-free bond.

## Callable-bond value decomposes cleanly

$$
V_{callable}=V_{option\text{-}free}-V_{call\ option}
$$

The issuer owns the call. Greater rate volatility usually increases the option's value and reduces the callable bond's value.

## Negative convexity appears when calls become likely

- At high yields, the call is unlikely and the bond behaves more like an option-free bond.
- As yields fall, expected maturity shortens.
- Price appreciation slows near the call price.

Duration can decline precisely when a noncallable bond's duration would remain high.

## Yield to worst is a convention—not an option model

Yield to worst selects the lowest calculated yield among relevant call, put, and maturity dates.

It does not model changing exercise probabilities, rate volatility, or the full term structure.

## A rate lattice supplies state-by-state discounting

A binomial tree provides short rates $r_{t,j}$ at future time $t$ and state $j$.

At every node, value depends on the two next-state values and the local discount rate.

## Backward induction values the holding decision

For coupon $C$, spread $s$, and risk-neutral up probability $q$:

$$
V^{hold}_{t,j}=\frac{C+qV_{t+1,j+1}+(1-q)V_{t+1,j}}{1+r_{t,j}+s}
$$

Work backward from maturity to today.

## The issuer applies a minimum rule

At an eligible call node:

$$
V^{callable}_{t,j}=\min\{V^{hold}_{t,j},K_t\}
$$

$K_t$ is the call price. If continuation value exceeds $K_t$, the issuer calls and caps the investor's value.

For an investor-owned put, the rule reverses:

$$V^{putable}_{t,j}=\max\{V^{hold}_{t,j},\text{Put price}_t\}$$

## A simple tree begins with terminal values

At maturity, after the final coupon convention is handled consistently:

$$V_T=F$$

The final coupon enters the preceding one-period holding value. Clear timing conventions prevent double counting.

## Work backward first without the call

At year 2 in a three-year example:

$$V^{straight}_{2,j}=\frac{C+qF+(1-q)F}{1+r_{2,j}}$$

This provides the continuation value against which the call price is compared.

## Then impose the call node by node

If continuation values are \$103.20 and \$99.40 with a \$101 call price:

- Low-rate node: $\min(103.20,101)=101$
- High-rate node: $\min(99.40,101)=99.40$

The option is exercised only where refinancing is valuable.

## Continue backward using capped node values

Earlier callable values use the already-capped next-state values:

$$V^{callable}_{t,j}=\frac{C+qV^{callable}_{t+1,j+1}+(1-q)V^{callable}_{t+1,j}}{1+r_{t,j}}$$

The exercise decision propagates backward into today's price.

## The embedded option cost is a price difference

$$V_{call\ option}=V_{straight}-V_{callable}$$

Value both securities on the same calibrated tree and with the same non-option spread assumptions.

## A production tree must fit today's curve

An arbitrary rate tree may illustrate mechanics but can misprice even option-free bonds.

A model-based tree is calibrated so its state prices reproduce observed discount factors before it is used for optionality.

## OAS removes modeled option cost from the spread

The option-adjusted spread is the constant spread added at every node that makes model value equal market price:

$$P_{market}=P_{model}(OAS)$$

OAS is solved numerically because price decreases as the trial spread increases.

## OAS supports more comparable spread analysis

- Callable and option-free bonds can be compared after modeled optionality.
- OAS still depends on the benchmark curve, volatility, model, and exercise assumptions.
- A wider OAS is not automatically a bargain; it may compensate for credit, liquidity, or model risk.

## Spread decomposition separates compensation from option cost

Conceptually:

$$\text{Observed spread}\approx\text{OAS}+\text{option cost in spread terms}$$

Option cost is model dependent and need not equal a simple yield-to-call adjustment.

## The callable/OAS demo is a reproducible workflow

The course demo `demo_callable_bond_oas.qmd` uses self-contained illustrative inputs to:

1. build a recombining short-rate tree,
2. price straight and callable bonds,
3. solve OAS from a target price,
4. calculate effective duration and convexity.

No external data file is required at render time.

## Effective duration reprices the entire option model

$$
D_{eff}=\frac{P_- - P_+}{2P_0\Delta y}
$$

$P_-$ and $P_+$ come from shifting the benchmark curve, rebuilding or recalibrating consistently, and repricing with the exercise rule.

## Effective convexity measures the model's curvature

$$
C_{eff}=\frac{P_-+P_+-2P_0}{P_0(\Delta y)^2}
$$

Callable bonds can exhibit low or negative effective convexity when falling rates materially increase call probability.

## OAS implementation is a chain of dependencies

Observed curve → calibrated rate model → volatility → exercise behavior → model price → solved OAS → effective risk

An error early in the chain can look like attractive spread later.

## A practical callable-bond review

1. Verify call schedule and timing conventions.
2. Inspect benchmark curve and volatility inputs.
3. Confirm tree calibration on option-free instruments.
4. Review exercise regions and option cost.
5. Stress OAS, duration, and convexity.

<div class="takeaway">OAS is not observed directly; it is the spread left after a model explains the option.</div>
